threat_assessment:
The table sees a four-mana Wizard, a fistful of Elves, and 36 Forests. Their read: fair stompy deck, ramping politely, no combo — and the record agrees with them. Zero contained combos, no game changers, a bracket floor of 1 against a target of 3. On paper you are the most ignorable deck at the table. Keep it that way. That paper is your camouflage, and your whole early game is spent keeping it accurate.

Your interaction is the untapped Forest. Stack 001 is the engine: Radagast's discount-and-flash resets every turn, so a four-player round hands you four windows and Wood Elves costs one green mana on an opponent's end step. So stop tapping out. Two open green is Frostfang, or Heroic Intervention, or nothing at all, and the table must price all three (strategy:multiplayer.pod-management). The card they cannot see does the deterrence work — your job is only to hold it back and pass.

Spring the first trap early and make it cheap for you, expensive for them. Stack 002 is the lesson plan: Frostfang flashed after blockers are declared turns damage already lined up into deathtouch, and one unblocked 1/1 pays you two cards on the way out. A player who loses two attackers to open mana stops attacking you for the rest of the night. That is the point of the trade — you are not buying creatures, you are buying a reputation.

Three signals flip you from ignored to archenemy, and you control all three. A fifth body — because everyone can count to Craterhoof. A visible finisher — Chord of Calling mana held up with a big board is an announcement, so do not hold eleven mana ostentatiously unless you intend to use it. And Selvala — she actually reads friendly, since she offers everyone draws; let them believe it, and do not lead her into open removal without a reason, because she is your only card of her class and the sim finds her in barely one game in six.

Do not pivot at four bodies. Stack 003 did the arithmetic: Craterhoof over four other bodies is 36 unblocked into one seat — loud, board-committing, and not lethal from 40. The fifth body clears the bar. The count is the trigger (strategy:pivot-point): five bodies plus a finisher in hand, and not before. A telegraphed pivot that falls four short is how a deflection deck elects itself archenemy for free.

Be honest about your own clock. The sim measures 3.64 bodies by turn six — the fifth does not arrive until about turn eight — and the finisher in hand 43% of the time. All floors, since it models neither the discount nor a single flash cast, but respect the shape: your pivot is usually not ready on turn six, so do not start acting like the threat on turn five. Every turn you look like the ramp deck running slightly behind, someone else eats the removal.

And when the count is right, embrace it completely. Flash the fifth body in on the end step before your turn — it swings that same turn, the haste-equivalence stack 006 verified — but cast the Behemoth in your own main phase. Stack 005 killed the cuter line: his pump dies at that end step's cleanup, so an end-step Craterhoof is a wrath-dodge, never a kill. Untap, cast, and point everything at the seat that can rebuild interaction fastest, with Heroic Intervention or Tyvar's Stand held for the vote you just called. There is no radar to be under once the Behemoth resolves, and you do not need one: you counted, they didn't. Four verified stacks and ten thousand goldfish runs say the plan is sound — now go play the games that prove it.
matchups:
Sort the table by one question: who can afford to ignore your open mana? The seats that can't will slow down and play worse (strategy:information). The seats that can are the ones these notes are for.

The flier deck is your worst axis, so say it out loud in your head and plan around it: Old Fat Spider's reach and Hornet Queen's five deathtouch fliers are the entire air defense. Do not plan to hold the sky — plan to race, and spend the Queen to buy the race time: flash her into their attack step and every swing after that is a losing trade for them. Hold Warg Tactics and Unforgiving Aim for the one flier that actually outraces you — the commander, the engine dragon — never the first bird that chips you. Pick Your Poison's flying mode makes each opponent sacrifice a flier of their choice, so fire it only when their best flier is their only flier. Meanwhile the ground is wide open in both directions: keep Toski and Frostfang connecting, and make the sky find its last points before your five bodies find theirs.

Against aggro you are the control seat (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Stack 002 already wrote the sign on your lawn — attack here and everything you lined up dies to a flashed Frostfang. Show it once, then let two open Forests do the job the card used to. Radagast's 2/5 blocks the early turns for free, and Guardian Augmenter flashes in to make him a hexproof 4/7 the moment someone tries to break the wall. Let the aggro seat spend itself into the other two players, then pivot the turn you stabilize — every passive turn past stable is a free draw step for somebody else (strategy:pivot-point).

Against sweeper control, fear the wrath early and welcome it late — the crossover card is Fecundity. Before your engines land, commit exactly as much board as wins before the sweeper arrives and not one body more (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). After Fecundity, the math flips: stack 004 verified that a Day of Judgment over your board pays you a card per creature — four wakes for you against their one — while Toski stands there indestructible and even Radagast's death is seen before he leaves for the command zone. Your rebuild is a feature, not a scramble: Radagast's first recast is six mana in a deck that finds ramp by turn six in 92% of runs, so redeploy worst-first, hold the finisher for their second sweeper, and flash the rebuild on end steps where a sorcery-speed wrath can never quite catch it — the one job stack 005 proves end-step deployment does best.

Against combo you are the beatdown, full stop — you lose every long game against inevitability (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). The toolkit is short: the clock, Collector Ouphe, Veil of Summer — and Deathgorge Scavenger when their engine lives in a graveyard, since he is a metronome body that eats the key card on the way in. Flash Ouphe in through Radagast's window on the combo player's own turn — stack 001 says the discount and the flash are live there — and hold Veil for the turn they point removal at Ouphe or disruption at your hand. Then be honest about the clock: stack 003 says one alpha strike takes one seat, not three, so the moment their proximity beats every board in sight, rank them archenemy (strategy:threat-assessment) and point all five bodies at the combo player, not the open one.

Against the artifact table you get to be the tax collector. Collector Ouphe switches off every activated mana rock at the table while your 36 Forests never notice he exists. Boseiju, Who Endures kills the key piece from your hand, and Life from the Loam brings it back — dredge Loam off any of your constant draw triggers, return Boseiju, channel again, with the cost shrinking for each legendary creature you control until it is one green mana per shot. Add Caustic Caterpillar, Wickerbough Elder, and Nantuko Vigilante as bodies that double as answers, and their engine pays you rent every turn it tries to restart. That is nine removal-class cards pointed at the one table that must respect all of them — collect.
how_it_wins:
The table sees mono-green and waits for the turn you tap out. That turn never comes. Radagast makes your first creature spell each turn cost {2} less and lets you cast it at instant speed — and "each turn" means all four of them, verified to the letter in stack 001, where Wood Elves cost a single {G} on an opponent's end step. Pass with mana open and deploy in whichever window hurts the table most.

The open mana is never just a bluff — a trap is in hand by turn six in 86% of games, so the table has to respect it every time. Ohran Frostfang flashed in after blockers are declared hands your attackers deathtouch in time for damage: on the record, a 1/1 killed a 6/6 and the turn drew two cards (stack 002). Fecundity turns their wrath into your hand — four cards off a Day of Judgment while indestructible Toski just stands there (stack 004). Attacking you is bad, removing you is bad, wrathing you is bad.

The kill is arithmetic, so do the arithmetic — and cast it at home. Craterhoof over four bodies is 36, four short of a 40-life seat (stack 003); over five bodies it is exactly 40 into one seat, and the verified line is your own precombat main, haste carrying the attack (stack 005). Flash the Hoof on an end step and the pump dies at that turn's cleanup — legal, and it kills nobody. The end step is for bodies, not finishers: everything you flash there wakes up attack-ready on your turn (stack 006).

The goldfish hands you floors, and your job is to beat them. Radagast lands turn four on average and by six in 94% of games; a metronome body is drawn by six in 92% of games; the average board is 3.6 bodies at turn six — short of the five the kill needs. The sim models neither the discount, nor flash casts, nor the ramp auras, so the real numbers climb every time you use a window. Use the windows.

combo_lines.001:
The case turns on two words: "each turn." The printed template "each of your turns" exists, and Radagast does not use it — so the count of creature spells you have cast zeroes at every untap, yours and theirs alike, a turn being a structural unit every player takes (CR 500.1, CR 102.1). One candour the record keeps and this column repeats: no single rule states that an each-turn count resets. The holding is derived from the ability's text plus the definition of a turn, and the checker judged the derivation sound exactly as hedged.

What resolves: Wood Elves for {G} on an opponent's end step, both halves of the ability — discount and as-though-flash — riding the same first spell (CR 601.3d, CR 601.2f), the fetched Forest entering untapped because it is put, not played (CR 305.4). Plain English: four windows per round in a four-player pod, one spell per window, and your second creature spell in any turn gets nothing.
combo_lines.002:
The clause that decides this is CR 604.2: a static ability functions from the moment its permanent is on the battlefield. Nothing asks whether Ohran Frostfang was present when attackers were declared — attacking status persists until the creature leaves combat or combat ends — so deathtouch attaches to damage already lined up. Toski's single point destroys the 6/6 as a state-based action (CR 704.5h); the 6 coming back is ignored outright, indestructible reading the lethal-damage check out of existence (CR 702.12b).

On the draws the record is exact. One creature dealt combat damage to a player, and two separate abilities each saw that one event once (CR 603.2): two cards, not four. The holding: the trap is real, the snake pays you for springing it, and the record supports nothing wider.
combo_lines.003:
The controlling rule is CR 608.2h: X is read once, when the effect applies, and Craterhoof Behemoth is on the battlefield to be counted — five creatures, +5/+5, trample. The arithmetic is the exhibit: 7 + 6 + 6 + 7 + 10 makes 36, against a seat on 40. The holding is negative and this column will not soften it: not lethal. The seat survives on 4.

The record allows one sentence past the miss: a fifth body on the battlefield before the trigger makes X six and the attackers six, which clears 40. On where that fifth body comes from, the record is silent — it prices the bar, not the route.
combo_lines.004:
Two clauses carry this one. Fecundity's trigger reads "a creature," unqualified — the record confirms it fires for every seat's dead, the drawback accepted in full (CR 603.2c, one event, seven occurrences). And CR 111.7's own parenthetical: a token's zone-change triggers fire before the token ceases to exist, so the Insect's death pays out like any other.

The count on the record: you draw 4, the two-creature seat draws 2, the wrath's own caster draws 1, the creatureless seat draws 0. Two footnotes worth their ink. Toski, indestructible, never dies and so never pays anyone (CR 702.12b). And Radagast genuinely dies before the command-zone move — that move is an optional state-based action after the fact (CR 903.9a) — so his death is one of your four. The wrath resolves, and yours is the largest hand at the table.
combo_lines.005:
The ruling everyone wants to skip is CR 514.2: every "until end of turn" effect ends at the cleanup of the turn that made it — that turn, not yours. So the record splits this line cleanly in two. The ambush cast is legal in every particular: the conditional flash (CR 601.3d), Castle Garenbrig's six activated mid-cast as a mana ability (CR 605.3a, CR 601.2g), all six restricted {G} landing on a creature spell (CR 106.6). And the pump it buys dies at that turn's cleanup, so the next morning's attack is 10 unpumped power. It kills nobody.

The verified kill is the unglamorous one: the same mana in your own precombat main, X counting six, haste carrying the fresh Behemoth — 40 trample damage, exactly lethal to one 40-life seat (CR 704.5a), per seat and never the pod. What the flash cast retains is defensive: a sorcery-speed wrath exists only in its caster's main phase (CR 117.1a), so the end step before your turn is the last safe moment to deploy. The holding: flash the Hoof to dodge, cast him at home to kill.
combo_lines.006:
One rule decides both prongs: CR 302.6. The attack clause and the tap-ability clause read the same test — continuous control since YOUR most recent turn began — and a creature entering on the end step before your turn predates that clock. Sakura-Tribe Elder, flashed for {G}, may attack at dawn and could activate any tap ability it had; the two permissions are exactly the pair haste grants (CR 702.10b, CR 702.10c), obtained by timing instead.

Two precisions the record keeps. The equivalence holds only from your turn onward — during the opponent's turn itself the arrival still fails the test, where a hasty creature would not. And the Elder's own sacrifice ability carries no tap symbol, so CR 302.6 never restricted it at all: it could have been activated the moment the spell resolved. The holding: the metronome's end-step bodies are never summoning-sick on the turn you need them.
combo_lines.007:
The clause is CR 109.2b: a description containing the word "spell" means a spell of that description on the stack. Chord of Calling on the stack is an instant, never a creature spell — and from that one clause, three refusals follow. Radagast's discount does not apply, and the turn's window is not consumed. Castle Garenbrig's six restricted {G} cannot pay for it (CR 106.6) — though the Castle's plain {T}: Add {G} could, a distinction the record insists on. Beast Whisperer does not draw.

The fourth refusal has its own clause: the fetched creature is put onto the battlefield, not cast (the glossary's definition of "cast"), so nothing that triggers on casting fires for Selvala's arrival either (CR 603.6a governs what does). Two figures close the record: X must be at least 3, because Selvala's mana value is 3 and Chord finds X or less; and having entered on the end step before your turn, she taps for mana on it (CR 302.6 — the stack 006 boundary). The holding: Chord refuses every gift and still does the one thing this deck cannot otherwise do at instant speed.

card_roles.Radagast of Rhosgobel: The clock the whole deck ticks to: your first creature spell each turn costs {2} less and casts at instant speed, and "each turn" means all four of them (stack 001). Spend a window every turn — a round where you only act on your own turn wasted three.
card_roles.Llanowar Elves: Turn-one Elves is turn-three Radagast — the sim lands him on three in about a third of games, almost always off a dork. Late, it is still a body toward five, and in stack 002 this exact 1/1 drew two cards.
card_roles.Elvish Mystic: Llanowar Elves' second copy. Same instruction: turn one, every time.
card_roles.Fyndhorn Elves: The third copy of the same card. Eight dorks is redundancy doing its job — play whichever one you drew.
card_roles.Birds of Paradise: The dork that stays home. Zero power means it never attacks; it taps, it blocks a flyer, and it counts under Craterhoof's X.
card_roles.Devoted Druid: Two mana a turn off one card when you need it — but each untap costs a -1/-1 counter, so it shrinks toward its own grave. Milk it on the big turn, not every turn.
card_roles.Scaled Nurturer: Read the fine print: the 2 life needs a Dragon spell, and this deck casts none. It is a {G} dork with a dead clause — count it as mana and a body, nothing more.
card_roles.Elvish Spirit Guide: Free mana from your hand, any time. This is how a window you look tapped-out for still produces a Frostfang — the bluff the table cannot price.
card_roles.Tireless Provisioner: Every land drop banks a Treasure, and banked mana is exactly what a deck spending on other players' turns wants. Take Treasure over Food unless you are dying.
card_roles.Sakura-Tribe Elder: Chump-block, then become a Forest. Trading it into a 6/6 costs the attacker a swing and costs you nothing — the deck's whole posture in one card. Flashed on the end step before your turn, it even wakes up attack-ready (stack 006).
card_roles.Wood Elves: The metronome's poster card: {G} on an opponent's end step, and the fetched Forest enters untapped — all of it verified in stack 001. Body, land, window: one card.
card_roles.Cultivate: One land tapped now, one in hand for the drop you would otherwise miss — land drops fall to 56% by turn six, and this is the patch.
card_roles.Kodama's Reach: Cultivate's twin. Cast it on your own turn — it is one of the few cards here that insists.
card_roles.Rampant Growth: Two mana, one tapped Forest. It is the turn-two play when the hand has no dork.
card_roles.Three Visits: Rampant Growth, except the Forest enters untapped — a real difference in a deck that wants {G}{G} open on everyone else's turn.
card_roles.Elvish Reclaimer: A one-drop that fetches Boseiju or Castle Garenbrig the turn you need them, and wears +2/+2 once three lands hit the graveyard. Satyr Wayfinder and Life from the Loam feed it.
card_roles.Satyr Wayfinder: Digs four for a land and stocks the graveyard that Elvish Reclaimer and Life from the Loam want full. The 1/1 is the tip, not the product.
card_roles.Life from the Loam: Three lands back for two mana, forever, and dredge turns dead draws into fuel. This is the card that makes missing land drops optional.
card_roles.Abundant Growth: One mana, draw a card, and a fixing clause mono-green never needs. It is a cantrip that remembers to be an enchantment; treat it as one.
card_roles.Utopia Sprawl: One mana that makes a Forest tap for two, from turn one. The sim models no auras at all, so every mana figure you have read is a floor this card quietly beats.
card_roles.Wild Growth: Same job as Utopia Sprawl on any land: one mana, and a land taps for two for the rest of the game.
card_roles.Fertile Ground: The two-mana copy of Wild Growth. Put it on the land you tap every turn.
card_roles.Beast Whisperer: A card per creature spell, and this deck casts one per window — up to four draws a round. Stack 003 shows it collecting even on the Craterhoof turn. Protect it accordingly.
card_roles.Toski, Bearer of Secrets: Cannot be countered, cannot be destroyed, must attack — and every connect anywhere on your team is a card. He skipped the wrath in stack 004 and shrugged off 6 damage in stack 002. Send him at the open seat every turn; that is what the must-attack clause is for.
card_roles.Selvala, Heart of the Wilds: The best engine card in the 99 and a class of exactly one — she shows up in 17% of games, so never plan around her. When she lands, a new biggest body draws its controller a card (usually you, with 35 creatures) and she taps for X equal to your greatest power. Chord of Calling fetches her at X=3 on the end step before yours, and she taps on your turn (stack 007).
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for everyone and a card per 4-power body entering. The static trample turns ordinary attacks into damage that always lands somewhere.
card_roles.Elemental Bond: A card per 3-power body entering. The dorks miss the bar; the middleweights clear it. Cast it before the bodies, not after — it only sees entries.
card_roles.Tribute to the World Tree: Never dead: a power-3 body draws, a smaller one takes two counters — three under Hardened Scales. Its {G}{G}{G} is the deck's heaviest cost, and 46 green sources make it routine.
card_roles.Fecundity: The wrath insurance, verified end to end: under Day of Judgment it drew you four and the wrath's caster one (stack 004). It is symmetric, so put it down when your board is the widest at the table and let everyone else fund your rebuild.
card_roles.Harmonize: Three cards, no conditions, no board required. It is the gas you cast on the turn the metronome has nothing worth flashing.
card_roles.Return of the Wildspeaker: An instant: end-step draw equal to your biggest non-Human power — Old Fat Spider makes that six — or +3/+3 to the team as a second overrun mode. Radagast, the Spider, and the hoof are all non-Human.
card_roles.Inspiring Call: Draws off +1/+1 counters and grants the counter-carriers indestructible at instant speed — Tribute to the World Tree and Hardened Scales load it. A wrath answer that pays you.
card_roles.Old Fat Spider: A 6/7 with reach that draws you a card whenever an opponent targets it, and power-2-or-less creatures cannot block it. Bad to attack into, bad to remove, bad to block — three taxes from one card.
card_roles.Ohran Frostfang: The flagship trap: flashed after blockers are declared, it hands your attackers deathtouch in time for damage — a 1/1 killed a 6/6 on the record (stack 002) — and every connect draws a card. Hold three mana and the table must price it into every block.
card_roles.Guardian Augmenter: Flash it in response to the kill spell: Radagast becomes a hexproof 4/7 and stays one. The whole deck is linear on his window — this is the insurance premium, pre-paid.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: The pivot's seatbelt. Hold it for the turn you commit the board — hexproof and indestructible through the wrath they were saving.
card_roles.Tyvar's Stand: Intervention for one creature with an {X} attached: X=0 protects Radagast for one mana, X=5 turns a blocked trade into a kill. The trap mana you keep open is also this.
card_roles.Veil of Summer: One mana that beats a counterspell, a kill spell, or a discard spell out of the blue and black seats — and draws a card doing it. Against those decks, the cheapest insurance in the 99.
card_roles.Sylvan Safekeeper: A land for a shroud, any time, no mana. The removal-proof board costs you land drops — Life from the Loam buys them back.
card_roles.Beast Within: Any permanent, instant speed, three mana. The 3/3 they get is real, so aim it at the combo piece or the lock, where a Beast is a bargain.
card_roles.Pick Your Poison: One mana, and every opponent sacrifices an artifact, an enchantment, or a flyer — pick the mode that hits all three seats at once.
card_roles.Unforgiving Aim: Green's answer to a flyer or an enchantment, with a 2/2 Elf as the fallback mode, so it is never dead. The flying mode matters: reach is thin here.
card_roles.Warg Tactics: Kill a flyer, or put a counter on your creature with trample and hexproof attached. The second mode feeds Inspiring Call and saves a body mid-combat.
card_roles.Caustic Caterpillar: A one-mana body holding a Disenchant. Cast it in a spare window and let it sit — the threat of activation taxes every artifact at the table.
card_roles.Nantuko Vigilante: Morph: a face-down 2/2 that flips for {1}{G} to eat an artifact or enchantment exactly when the target shows. The table never knows which trap the facedown is.
card_roles.Wickerbough Elder: It enters a 3/3 and grows to 4/4 by destroying an artifact or enchantment — removal that leaves a body behind. Take the counter off only when there is something worth killing.
card_roles.Collector Ouphe: Activated abilities of artifacts stop, and the Sol Ring seats lose their rocks. Mind the friendly fire: your own Treasures and Food go dark too. Cast it when their artifacts matter more than Tireless Provisioner's.
card_roles.Mirkwood Pathmaker: Power and toughness equal to your lands: modest when it arrives, a 7/7 by the pivot. Cheap now, big exactly when Craterhoof asks how big.
card_roles.Scute Swarm: Every land is a body, and past six lands every land is another Scute Swarm. This is where the fifth body comes from — and stack 003 says the fifth body is the difference between 36 and lethal.
card_roles.Eternal Witness: Buys back whatever the game took: the countered finisher, the spent Intervention, the dead Frostfang. A metronome body with a receipt.
card_roles.Fauna Shaman: A spare body in, the exact card out, every turn — with 35 creatures the discard is never a real cost. Loop toward Craterhoof when the board says pivot, toward Caustic Caterpillar when it says stop.
card_roles.Chord of Calling: Any body, instant speed, and convoke lets the board pay for its own reinforcement. Know what it refuses (stack 007): no Radagast discount — though the window survives untouched — no Castle Garenbrig six, no Beast Whisperer draw, and the fetched creature arrives uncast, triggering nothing that reads "cast."
card_roles.Hardened Scales: Every counter event pays one extra: Tribute's two become three, Warg Tactics' one becomes two. One mana — cast it early, because it only pays going forward.
card_roles.Craterhoof Behemoth: The pivot button, and the record is precise about pressing it: cast him in your own precombat main — X counts itself, and five bodies before him is exactly 40 trample into one seat, while four leaves a survivor at 4 (stacks 005, 003). Flashed on an end step, the pump dies at that turn's cleanup: flash him only to dodge a wrath, never to attack.
card_roles.Overwhelming Stampede: The second hoof: trample plus +X/+X where X is your greatest power, so any 5-power body makes it a team-wide +5. This is the finisher redundancy the pivot math demands.
card_roles.Pathbreaker Ibex: Craterhoof on a repeating trigger: every attack, trample and +X/+X off your biggest power. Protect it the turn before the pivot, not after.
card_roles.Boseiju, Who Endures: A Forest that answers an artifact, an enchantment, or a nonbasic land at instant speed — and your legends discount it, so with Radagast out Channel costs {G}. Fetch it with Elvish Reclaimer the moment the table shows a target.
card_roles.Castle Garenbrig: Six green in one activation, spendable only on creature spells and creature abilities — it pays for Craterhoof, never for Chord of Calling. Untapped as long as you control a Forest, which is always.
card_roles.Gemstone Mine: Three activations, then it sacrifices itself, and the any-colour clause buys nothing in mono-green. Treat it as a short-term untapped source and spend it early.
card_roles.Khalni Garden: Enters tapped and pays you a 0/1 Plant — a chump block, a convoke tapper, and a body under Craterhoof's X on a stalled board.
card_roles.Slippery Karst: A tapped Forest early, a fresh card for {2} late. Cycle it the moment land drops stop mattering.
card_roles.Thriving Grove: Enters tapped, and the colour it names is wasted here. Sequence it on a turn you were not spending anyway.
card_roles.Forest: Thirty copies — enough that Wood Elves, Three Visits, Utopia Sprawl, and Castle Garenbrig's untapped clause never miss.
card_roles.Bala Ged Recovery // Bala Ged Sanctuary: A land when you need the drop, a Regrowth when you need the card back — the tapped-land mode is the price of never being dead. Default to the land side early; the recovery side exists for the finisher the graveyard is holding.
card_roles.Arasta of the Endless Web: Every instant or sorcery an opponent casts hands you a 1/2 reach Spider — width that accrues on other people's turns, which is the only kind of turn this deck respects. Against the spellslinger seat she is a body per spell; against everyone she is reach the flyers must price.
card_roles.Hornet Nest: A 0/2 nobody sane touches: every point of damage it takes becomes that many 1/1 flying deathtouch Insects. It cannot attack — it sat out both swings in stack 005 — so its whole job is making your half of the board a minefield.
card_roles.Dawn's Light Archer: A trap with the flash printed on: a 4/2 reach body that ambushes a flyer mid-combat without spending Radagast's window. Power 4 fires Garruk's Uprising on the way in.
card_roles.Saryth, the Viper's Fang: Read her two halves by tap state: your tapped creatures — the attackers — all have deathtouch, and your untapped ones at home hide behind hexproof. The {1}, {T} untap is a lever: reset Selvala, or move a body from one gift to the other.
card_roles.Deathgorge Scavenger: The 99's only answer to an opponent's graveyard — everything else here that touches a graveyard recurs your own cards — and it exiles on entry and again on every attack. A power-3 body besides, so Elemental Bond and Tribute pay out on arrival.
card_roles.Hornet Queen: Five bodies from one card — the biggest single jump toward the five the kill math demands — and all five fly with deathtouch, so the same card is your insurance against a mass attack. Seven mana at retail, {2}{G}{G}{G} in a Radagast window.
card_roles.Ravenous Sailback: A modal trap on a power-4 body: cast in your own main, the haste mode makes a surprise attacker; flashed into a window, the other mode eats an artifact or enchantment. Either way it is never dead, and power 4 pays the Garruk's Uprising toll.

mulligan:
Keep two to four lands and one accelerant — that is the whole rule, and the sim backs it: 81.4% of first sevens are keeps, and kept hands cluster at two to four lands. A one-mana dork is turn-three Radagast; he lands on three in about a third of games and on four in more than half, nearly always off an Elves.

The second thing to want is something to do at instant speed: an Ohran Frostfang, a Heroic Intervention, a Wood Elves to flash into someone's end step. A hand that plays draw-go from turn three is a keep. A hand that must tap out on its own turn every turn is playing someone else's deck.

Ship three shapes. Two or more five-plus drops — Craterhoof Behemoth is the payoff, not the plan. All lands and dorks with nothing to hold up. And any hand you are keeping because Selvala, Heart of the Wilds is in it — she is a class of one, so she is a bonus, never a reason. Everything else, keep: this deck averages 0.22 mulligans, and it earns that by not needing much.

That gap is the binding constraint: the diagnosis walked all sixteen axes and found the mana over-supplied (52 sources against a Burgess target of 36), the trap machinery near-universal, and board width the number every other weakness sits downstream of. The Short List's first job is bodies.

The second number is zero: sweepers. The traps trade one-for-one, and nothing in these 99 resets a resolved wide board — the one coverage hole open. The diagnosis names the shapes that close it in colour: Whiptongue Hydra is the one the role taxonomy can see; Ezuri's Predation is the one the deck actually wants.

The bracket-4 door, for the record, is not a Game Changer question — no card here carries the tag. It is two specific cards wide: Nissa, Resurgent Animist and Springheart Nantuko, each a recorded half of a two-card infinite — Nissa with Springheart, Springheart with Tireless Provisioner, who is already aboard. Thirty-six land copies across seven names, and thirty of them say Forest. Four enter tapped, three of those unconditionally — an 11% tap rate against the usual one-in-three budget, about as far under budget as a manabase gets. The colour ledger is one line long: pip share 1.00, source share 1.00. Mono-green leaves nothing to arbitrate.

The target says G36 and the lands supply exactly 36 — met on the nose before the ten creature-side producers lift the total to 46. Lands alone put the deck on curve 90.6% of the time; count the dorks and it is 97.4%. Eighty-two green pips across 63 cards, and nothing asks for more than three at once — the triple-{G} costs, Tribute to the World Tree, Hornet Queen, and Craterhoof Behemoth, are what the 46 exist for.

What the dorks actually buy is the commander's clock. Mean available mana reaches 4.15 on turn four; Radagast costs four, and his mean cast is turn 4.0. Land drops decay from 91% on turn three to 56% by turn six, which is why the back half of the ramp package is shaped like recovery — Life from the Loam, Satyr Wayfinder, and the Cultivate pair's land-in-hand.

Two footnotes the figures cannot show. Castle Garenbrig's six-mana burst spends only on creature spells and creature abilities, and the record settles it both ways: it pays for a flashed Craterhoof (stack 005) and never for Chord of Calling (stack 007). And the three ramp auras appear in neither the hypergeometrics nor the goldfish arithmetic, so every number above is a floor: this manabase measures better than it reads, and it already reads clean.
